meta.title: Who really said "Inside every old person is a young person wondering what happened"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Terry Pratchett used it in Moving Pictures (1990), but Quote Investigator traces the line to critic Dan Sullivan in the Los Angeles Times, 1976.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Inside every old person is a young person wondering what happened'?
meta.ogDescription: Pratchett wrote it in Moving Pictures (1990), but it was already a saying. The earliest close match is Dan Sullivan, Los Angeles Times, 1976.

answer.label: Not Pratchett’s coinage — earliest known: Dan Sullivan
answer.sourceLine: The earliest close match known to Quote Investigator ↗ is Sullivan’s Los Angeles Times article of 8 August 1976: “inside every old person there is a young one wondering what happened.” Terry Pratchett really did use the popular wording in Moving Pictures (1990), but QI finds the saying was already in circulation by then.

source.heading: The earliest known source

docMeta.dd: Moving Pictures (Discworld 10), first published by Gollancz in 1990

source.excerpt: If you looked through the eyeholes, you saw that Sylvia had very young eyes, and it almost seemed a reminder that inside every old person there is a young one wondering what happened.
trail: 1976: Dan Sullivan, writing in the Los Angeles Times about the Los Angeles Mask Theater, describes “a young one wondering what happened.” This is the earliest close match known to Quote Investigator ↗.

1979–1980: Ashleigh Brilliant’s syndicated “Potshots” cartoon prints “Inside every older person, there’s a younger person wondering what happened.” It reappears in his 1980 collection, where the cartoon carries the year 1978 (QI ↗).

1990: Terry Pratchett uses the line in Moving Pictures ↗, in a passage about the Unseen University wizards acting like young students. His publisher’s Wit and Wisdom of Discworld ↗ page lists it as coming “From, MOVING PICTURES.”

2001–2002: Usenet posts credit gospel singer Cora Harvey Armstrong with versions ending “wondering what the heck happened” and “wondering what the hell happened.” QI treats these as later variants (QI ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is Quote Investigator’s transcription of Sullivan’s review. In it, a young actress plays an elderly woman, Sylvia, wearing a mask. Sullivan wrote “a young one”. The exact popular wording, “. . . inside every old person is a young person wondering what happened,” is the one QI quotes from Pratchett’s Moving Pictures (1990).

author.name: Dan Sullivan
author.heading: The critic behind the line
author.metaLine: 1935–2022 · American theater critic, Los Angeles Times
author.bio: Dan Sullivan was an American theater critic. He wrote for the Los Angeles Times, The New York Times, the Minneapolis Tribune and the St. Paul Pioneer Press. He became the Los Angeles Times’ chief theater critic in 1969 and held that post for 22 years. He also directed the Eugene O’Neill National Critics Institute and co-founded the American Theater Critics Association. In a 1976 review of a masked-theater troupe, he wrote the earliest close match to this saying that Quote Investigator ↗ has found.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: This line is credited to several well-known names. Each one used or spread it, but Quote Investigator ↗ found an earlier source for all of them.

items.why: Pratchett did use these exact words in Moving Pictures (1990). His publisher’s Wit and Wisdom of Discworld page ↗ also promotes the line as his. But QI ↗ finds the saying was already in circulation before 1990, going back to 1976.
Brilliant printed the “older person … younger person” version in a November 1979 “Potshots” cartoon and in his 1980 book. That is still after Sullivan’s 1976 article (QI ↗).
Usenet posts in 2001 and 2002 credit the gospel singer with “wondering what the heck happened” and a version about women. QI calls these later instances of a saying that already existed (QI ↗).

Irish comedian Hal Roach printed it as “A THOUGHT” in a book that existed by February 1987. Barbara Johnson introduced it in 1990 with “They say,” treating it as a saying that was already around (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest close match Quote Investigator ↗ has found is Dan Sullivan’s Los Angeles Times article of 8 August 1976. QI names Sullivan as the leading candidate for creator. Pratchett’s 1990 use is real, but it came later.

context.heading: Why Pratchett gets the credit
lead: The Pratchett credit isn’t invented. The popular wording does appear in Moving Pictures, the tenth Discworld novel, and his publisher’s quote collections pass it along under his name. What the credit leaves out is that Pratchett was using a line people already knew. Quote Investigator ↗ found it in a cartoon, a South Dakota newspaper column, a birthday card and an Irish joke book, all before 1990.

The earliest close match came from a theater review. Sullivan was watching a young actress wear the mask of an old woman. He saw young eyes behind the old face and turned the image into a general remark about aging.
context.detailsSummary: A related saying with a different ending
detailsBody: A sister saying, “Inside every old person there is a young person trying to get out,” has its own history. Quote Investigator traces it to an older pattern about fat men and thin men, and finds a partial match in a 1962 column by Mary Courtland (QI ↗).
According to QI, the 1976 Sullivan citation was first recorded in The Dictionary of Modern Proverbs (Yale University Press, 2012).
